title: Advance requests built beside the staff ledger
story: A new advance-request feature reused older ledger patterns. 544 unit tests passed. An Opus audit the next day found stacking races, an actor foreign-key clash and an auto-approve failure.
entry: staff_ledger: append-only staff money. Unsigned amount with a database CHECK. Corrections void and re-log, never edit. Balances only through one repository function. Writes idempotent on a unique client_id. New money columns end in _minor.
steps: CLAUDE.md already summarised the earlier tables when 0042 began. The shapes were in the window before any lookup.
Building 0042 raised no error. The design's triggers do not cover request stacking or a system actor.
'Exactly-once disbursement' shares words with the ledger entry. No query asks whether two requests can stack.
Four partial matches come back. The other design shows at most one lead and one candidate, so pieces drop out.
The main session pulls the cards into its own window. One session builds the slice.
The working step, a pre-minted client id that becomes the ledger row's id, is in no entry. Reusing the old actor key with a new 'auto' actor causes a foreign-key violation.
544 unit and 7 integration tests passed. The stacking race and auto-approve failure were invisible. An Opus audit added guards next day.
Nothing failed during the task, so nothing was handed up. The fixes came from a later audit outside any ladder.
Stored at 'solved', the entry holds the half-right design. The other design's write rule would store nothing. The owner's rule stores the flawed version.
Turning a pay setting on makes the %-of-accrued cap non-binding. The naming rule does not say which style a new key follows.

title: Latest-row-wins ordering by created_at
story: Two writes in one transaction tie on created_at. A real-Postgres CI test caught it in 14 minutes. Four hours later the new rule pointed the next table, 0041, the wrong way.
entry: job_event.seq gives a total order: backfill with row_number, create a sequence, then NOT NULL and UNIQUE. Also: latest-row-wins tables must not order by created_at, because now() ties inside one transaction. Use a monotonic seq.
worked: The real-database test caught the tie in 14 minutes, with a check that reproduced the cause.
steps: The task, CLAUDE.md and tenancy code held the pattern. The seq pattern lived in 0027's code.
Nothing triggers while designing. The CI failure is a trigger, so a lookup runs only after one CI round.
'Latest row wins per key' shares little with 0027's words. The CI error is a value assertion and names neither now() nor created_at.
0027's entry is the right neighbour but holds no reason against created_at. Its own backfill orders by created_at. At 0041 the fresh entry is a wrong match.
The main session is where the design happens.
At 0041 'use a DB sequence' breaks the chain: gaps on rollback, no hash link. 'Never created_at' flags 0041's backfill, which is correct.
The real-Postgres CI test caught the tie in 14 minutes. The check reproduces the cause.
A cheap model facing a wrong-value assertion would escalate. The strong model fixed it in 14 minutes in one commit. Any rung costs more.
The other design stores nothing here. The owner's rule stores it, and its general form is too broad for 0041 four hours later.
Within four hours the entry points the next table the wrong way on both its seq and its backfill order.

title: WhatsApp consumer on an old outbox cursor
source: Migrations 0027 and 0034; commit da988e2; HANDOFF line 303
story: The new real sender used an old rule: a missing cursor starts at zero and drains all history. Nothing failed while the dispatcher was off. An audit found it 20 days later.
entry: Transactional outbox. job_event.seq gives a gap-free global order. dispatch_cursor holds one row per consumer. run_dispatch_once reads past last_seq and advances only past accepted events. A scheduler runs it behind enable_dispatcher, default OFF. The WhatsApp consumer is log-only for now.
steps: 0034 was built the same day as 0027, both by Fable. The dispatcher code was fresh.
Nothing fails, because the dispatcher is off. No trigger exists for 'a new consumer on an old cursor'.
The builder asked about double-send on replay. The hazard answers a different question: what does the first run do with history?
It returns 0027's entry, the right neighbour, without the start-from-zero warning. That is harmless for a log-only consumer.
The main session window holds it.
The hazard exists only in the merge: an old default, a new real sender, and a permanent first decision per job and kind. Neither parent entry holds it.
Tests passed, including the unique guard. Nothing tested a first run against history. An audit found it 20 days later. The fix landed 24 days later.
No failure was visible, so nothing went up. The finder was a later audit.
The stored conclusion would be 'enable_dispatcher stays safe to flip'. That is wrong, and fetched by anyone about to flip it.
After 0046 the other design has an action handle and diff warnings that fired on 13 of 154 past commits. 'Seed at head' is right for WhatsApp only.

title: Database locks that were too weak
source: Slice sessions S01, S03, S04, S07; D04-06; F-S02-2
story: Slice sessions copied an item lock and a 32-bit hash lock. Deadlocks were retried silently. An Opus review and a staging drill found the faults. The kernel later went 64-bit but two copies stayed 32-bit.
entry: Kernel run_command: one transaction per command. Keys serialized with pg_advisory_xact_lock and hashtext. Retry only on 40001/40P01, at most three times. Open item: hashtext is 32-bit, so a collision serializes unrelated keys. Item lock is select_for_update.
worked: The slice's own conventions file captured the rule the same day.
steps: Slice sessions open on large context. S07 read 392,125 characters in nine minutes before its lock. S04 averaged about 231k cached tokens per call.
Writing a lock raises no error. The kernel retries deadlocks. select_for_update is too common to pass the selectivity gate.
'Lock the item before posting' finds a lock of the right shape and wrong strength. The key-share fact sits under a test remark that a lock-order query does not reach.
The best matches are the defect sources. The sibling is the problem.
The row entered S07's main window nine minutes before the copy, with no compaction between.
S07 wrote the 32-bit lock anyway. The row said 'P3' and named an owner elsewhere. S04 wrote the item lock row FOR UPDATE.
Tests pass, and deadlocks are retried. An Opus review found S04's deadlock by tracing. A staging drill found the hash collision.
The higher tier caught it as a diff reviewer, not because the builder failed and handed up. The builder never knew.
S04 wrote a decision record and a conventions line the same day, naming the sites still wrong. The conventions file did the capture.
S03 merged before S04 learned the rule, and was fixed five days later. The kernel went 64-bit on 11-06. Two copies are still 32-bit. One reversal keeps FOR UPDATE on purpose.

title: Mobile offline queues after the jobs outbox
story: The first outbox deleted any write answered with a non-network error. Later queues copied the lesson. The presence queue lacked a 4xx test for three days. Shared code then fixed it.
entry: Mobile outbox v2. A definitive 4xx goes to a visible failed list with Retry or Discard, never auto-deleted. 5xx, 429 and timeouts retry. 401 pauses the queue until re-login. Tag each item with the signed-in tech.
worked: Later queues reused the shared classification from their first commit and chose park or drop correctly.
steps: The presence task and attendance code were in the window. The outbox lesson lived in the outbox code and the commit body.
Nothing fails. A 403 or 422 leaves a 'pending' badge forever with no error to look up.
The builder's words, 'offline presence outbox', share 'offline' and 'outbox' with the entry.
Presence and punches have the same contract. Pings are similar but not the same, because they are droppable by design.
Presence must park a definitive 4xx. Pings must drop it while 401 still stops the drain. The ping author broke the rule on purpose but not the classification.
Jest tests with a mocked network passed, but none sent a 4xx. The ping gap was found five hours later. The presence gap lived three days.
No failure was visible, so nothing went up.
c27bb39 turned the lesson into shared code. CLAUDE.md states the contract and its two droppable exceptions.
Later queues imported the shared check from their first commit and chose park or drop correctly.
